title: D!ck measure contest. Do you think which background will likely success create better game with AI?
author: Free-Version-2746
selftext:
AI democratization gamedev

Which one you think most likely success:

\-Programmer

\-Artist

\-Musician

\-Filmmakers

\-Content creator

\-Project Managers

comments.author: EliasWick
comments.body: Well, neither. It's tech artists. (Yes, I am biased).

replies.author: Free-Version-2746
replies.body: Is tech artists the guy create shader for the game?

replies.author: EliasWick
replies.body:
Yes, and pipelines, automation, asset optimization, tools, procedural content creation, exporters, vfx.

New developers don't understand how powerful it is to know shaders and GLSL / HLSL. I can basically make a full game using like 95% shaders, and just feeding it some other data like inputs.

comments.author: Revolutionary-Skin97
comments.body:
1. Full Stack Indie Developers (Front end back-end) who has a game in their heads waiting to happen.  
2. Senior Artist who already has their signature art.  
3. Senior Game Designers

not in any particular order but this are the 3 i think who'll excel in the coming years.

replies.author: Due_Answer_4230
replies.body: In general, if you already have a big cache of your own prior good work to point an AI at and say “like that”, you’re going way further way faster. You can also direct AI away from mistakes and dead ends in your area of expertise. There are also areas where AI isn’t as well developed, like sound design.

comments.author: TheReviewerWildTake
comments.body:
Assuming we are talking about people who have exactly ZERO knowledge of other fields (which is often not the case in indie scene), then programming is the most valuable skill to have.   
Albeit, saying "programming" -  is a bit vague, so it is more like "coding in your framework\\engine of choice".  
  
You can generate music, art, trailers and such, and kind of keep them on the level of placeholders for a while, but if you are unable to fix issues, compatibility, bugs, performance, unable to react to feedback and can\`t make clean fixes etc. you are basically can\`t outgrow small scale projects (where AI does not fck things up).  
  
This is why all those massive "clone games" we see here and there, are dead on arrival, and all die in beta, because nobody can fix that tech mess and nobody can polish something that falls apart everyone AI touches it...

Ppl can cope with poor art, but if your game crashes and your response to fixing technical issues is "sorry, my AI can\`t fix it" ?  
Yeah, that is insta Goodbye .

Basically, technical side is a hard-locking isue, while all the other sides are more like "soft-locks".  
  
With bad marketing you are "soft-locked" out of popularity, but your game still works and is playable, and can be picked up.  
  
With poor music you are soft-locked out of audiophiles and their preferences, but other ppl can still value it.  
  
With bad tech  - everyone just shits on you...

If you want to see how bad is technical issues for the game\`s image\\rep - check what happens when company has a buggy launch. So many games had "mixed" reviews based mainly on poor performance.  
  
Or take a witcher 3 remaster for example, that is receiving tons of negative reviews right now due to amount of tech issues..  
Let alone some indie game with no fans and no trust reserves.
